stimulus.text: Historian Lynn Dumenil describes the 1920s as a decade when 'modernity collided with tradition' — new consumer goods, new freedoms for women, and new mass media unsettling older Protestant, small-town certainties.

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of social or cultural change in the 1920s.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of that change.
C. Briefly explain ONE example of resistance to social or cultural change in the 1920s.
exemplar: Mass consumer culture arrived: radios, refrigerators, and automobiles bought on installment plans, sold by a new advertising industry, reshaped daily life.
Women claimed new freedoms — the flapper, the vote (1920), and public figures from Dorothy Parker to Aimee Semple McPherson embodying female voices in literature and religion.
Resistance was fierce: Prohibition, the Scopes trial over evolution, the reborn Ku Klux Klan, and the 1924 immigration quotas defended a 'traditional' America against the new culture.

Carnegie argues that great wealth, concentrated in a few hands, is not an evil but a problem to be managed: the rich have a duty to administer their fortunes so that rich and poor remain bound in social harmony.
Carnegie himself acted on this creed, funding thousands of public libraries, universities, and foundations - philanthropy on a scale that made him the era's leading example of the Gospel of Wealth.

Critics such as labor leaders and Populists argued that Carnegie's philosophy justified exploitation: at Homestead (1892) his managers used armed force against striking workers, suggesting 'brotherhood' did not extend to the factory floor.
parts: A. Briefly describe Carnegie's view of concentrated wealth as expressed in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE way Carnegie or another industrialist acted on the philosophy described in the excerpt.
C. Briefly explain ONE criticism leveled against the philosophy described in the excerpt.

stimulus.attribution: Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth' (the Gospel of Wealth), North American Review, June 1889.
stimulus.text: The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.

exemplar: The poster shows women as capable industrial workers, directly challenging the idea that factory work was men's work and urging women to take wartime jobs.
The federal government expanded women's employment through wartime production needs and agencies like the War Manpower Commission, drawing some six million women into the workforce.

After the war, many women were pushed out of industrial jobs as returning veterans reclaimed them, and popular culture renewed pressure on women to return to domestic roles - though women's labor-force participation never fell back to prewar levels.
parts: A. Briefly describe the poster's message about women's roles during World War II.
B. Briefly explain ONE way the federal government expanded women's economic opportunities during World War II.
C. Briefly explain ONE way women's wartime gains were limited or reversed after 1945.

stimulus.attribution: Described from the 1943 'We Can Do It!' poster by J. Howard Miller.
stimulus.text: The poster shows a strong, determined woman in a red bandana and blue work shirt, rolling up her sleeve and flexing her arm beneath the words 'We Can Do It!' Her direct gaze and muscular pose present female factory labor as powerful and patriotic.
